Read the room.

A crate map for warm-ups, rollers, peak-hour pressure, afters and the soft landing. Less filing-cabinet genre talk; more where a tune lands and what it does to the floor.

A library for the long night

What are 6,419 tracks for? Not for display — a collection this size is not a trophy wall, it is a working instrument. Every library of recorded music is really a diary of the hours its owner wanted to shape: the nights they wanted to carry, the rooms they wanted to hold, the mornings they wanted to survive. Read this way, the archive answers its own question. It is for playing music to people, in order, with care — for making nights that begin warm and end somewhere honest.

The first thing the numbers confess is the shape of an arc. Forty-four percent of the collection — 3,223 tracks — is built for the warm-up, the hours when the room is filling and everything is still possible. Another 30.4 percent is peak-time ammunition. Fourteen-point-eight percent belongs to the afterhours, that grey-blue window when only the faithful remain. This is a front-loaded library, weighted toward beginnings. Most collections are top-heavy with bangers; this one is richest in the tracks that open rooms. That tells you who assembled it: not the headliner who arrives at the drop, but the selector who got there early, who has spent years learning that the hardest and most generous hour in a DJ's life is the first one, when nobody is dancing yet and the night could go anywhere. The energy distribution agrees — the collection's most common energy is 2, not 5.

And then there is the native tongue. Nearly half the archive speaks one language in three dialects: Deep House (1,429 tracks), Tech House (910), Organic House (828). This is the vocabulary the collector dreams in. The deep house wing is warm, smooth, soulful, atmospheric, introspective — late-night music that leans close and tells the truth quietly. The tech house wing is the counterweight: punchy, rolling, club-driving, pure momentum — the engine room of the whole operation. And organic house is the sunlight: organic, percussive, melodic, laid-back, sunlit — music for open-air hours, for when the light comes back and nobody wants to go home. Between them these three shelves hold the collector's entire philosophy of the dance floor: build it warm, drive it hard, let it breathe.

But a night does not end at the peak, and neither does this library. The afterhours shelf — over a thousand tracks — is where the collection gets strange and serious. Minimal / deep tech: stripped, hypnotic, dubby, rolling into the small hours. Progressive house: gradual, evolving, emotional, a journey you agree to take without knowing the destination. Melodic house and techno: cinematic, moody, sophisticated — music that asks for your full attention and repays it. This is the 2 a.m. mind, the part of the collector that never stopped being curious about what happens after the lights come up halfway. The night deepens, and the collection's vocabulary deepens with it.

Then morning. Six hundred and thirty-three tracks for the chill-out and the comedown — the archive's gentlest corner. Lo-fi: mellow, dusty, nostalgic, hazy, warm as a worn photograph. Chill jazz led by Vanilla's 22 entries: smooth, jazzy, sophisticated, late-night in a completely different key. Ambient, dominated by The Luna Lounge's 46 tracks — the single deepest artist commitment in the entire library — spacious, meditative, abstract: the exhale after the long night. Beyond the club entirely: bachata that is romantic, sensual, swaying; country that is storytelling, heartfelt, honest; worship music reverent and communal; reggae sunny and easy. A person with a whole life, not just a DJ booth — but every shelf is chosen by the same ear, the one that hears warmth first.

So what kind of listener — what kind of DJ — is this? The signature artists tell the final part of the story. Retza (27) and the deep house faithful: selectors' selectors. Ben Rau (29), the minimal afterhours technician. Mark Henning (25) and Dennis Cruz (24), precision peak-time machinery. These are not chart names; they are workers' names, producers whose records you know because you were standing in front of a soundsystem at the right hour. The collection is not a fan's scrapbook — it is a craftsperson's toolkit, built track by track across years of listening with intent, each record answering the question: when would I reach for this?

And that is what it is for: a life organized around the belief that music is most powerful when aimed at a specific hour of a specific night — that the right record at 11 p.m. and the right record at 5 a.m. are different moral acts. The collector is the person who holds the whole arc in their head at once: the warm-up's patience, the peak's release, the afterhours' devotion, the morning's tenderness. Fifty-six genres, more than six thousand tracks, every one filed under a single unspoken conviction — that a night, played well, is a kind of care.

The moments

These five moments are the spine of the collection: the real shape of the taste, measured in tracks reached for at each hour of the night.

Warm-Up 3,223 tracks

The collection's great love affair. Nearly half the archive — 44.2 percent of everything — is music for the hours when the room is empty and then, gradually, isn't. This is the deep house ocean (1,350 of its tracks live here), the organic house sunlight (819), the eclectic miscellany that refuses a shelf but always seems to fit the first hour (544). Warm-up music is the hardest to choose and the easiest to underestimate: it asks nothing of the listener yet and gives everything. The collector's deepest instinct is generosity at low volume. These are the tracks for when the lights are still up and the night is a promise nothing has broken yet. A library this weighted toward beginnings belongs to someone who believes the opening hour is not the waiting room for the main event.

Peak-Time 2,215 tracks

Thirty-point-four percent of the archive, and the difference between this shelf and the last is the difference between an invitation and a command. Peak-time is tech house with its momentum and punch (898 tracks), house music at its most classic and jacking (490), the pop-dance crossover with its singalong brightness (196). The energy climbs to 3 and 4; the vibe words turn punchy, rolling, club-driving, celebratory, euphoric. This is the hour the warm-up was building toward — hands up, voices up, the room moving as one animal. But the collection gives peak-time its due without worshipping it: two thousand weapons oiled and ready, yet the peak is a visitor here, not a resident.

Afterhours 1,080 tracks

Fourteen-point-eight percent, and the most serious room in the house. Afterhours is where the collection stops performing and starts confessing: minimal / deep tech, stripped and hypnotic and dubby (376 tracks); progressive house, gradual and evolving and emotional (240); melodic house and techno, cinematic and moody (187); electronica, textural and leftfield (128). The energy settles at 3 — not exhausted, not frantic, but locked in. The vibe words are the archive's most poetic: hypnotic, late-night, journey, deep, underground, warehouse. This music is for the hours when the crowd has thinned to the true believers, when the DJ plays for the dancers who stayed. It asks for patience and rewards it with transcendence. If the warm-up shelf is the collector's generosity, the afterhours shelf is their devotion.

Chill-Out 633 tracks

The morning after, filed with love. Lo-fi leads — 250 tracks of mellow, dusty, nostalgic, hazy warmth, music that sounds like a memory of a good day. Beside it: jazz-hop, jazzy and laid-back; chill jazz, smooth and sophisticated; ambient, spacious and meditative, with The Luna Lounge's 46 tracks forming the single deepest artist run in the archive. Even country drifts in here — storytelling, heartfelt, honest — and reggae, sunny and easy. The chill-out shelf is the collector at their most human: no dance floor to command, no arc to complete, just records for sitting still. These are tracks for the drive home, the kitchen at dawn, the headphones on a slow Sunday. A collection that files 633 tracks under rest is a collection assembled by someone who understands that the night only means something because the morning exists.

Closing 136 tracks

The smallest shelf and the most deliberate. Closing is a specialist's moment — the last record, the lights coming up, the thing people will remember on the way out. Worship music anchors it: 31 tracks, uplifting, reverent, communal, hopeful — the only genre in the archive defined by what it gives rather than what it takes. Around it, fragments from across the collection: trance's euphoric hands-up farewells, eclectic outliers, deep house's final introspective murmurs. One hundred and thirty-six tracks is not a crate, it is a shortlist — a few ways to say goodbye, but the right ones. The closing shelf is the archive's benediction: after the warmth, the peak, the devotion, the rest — a quiet amen.

Deep House 1,429 tracks

This is the archive's home ground — the largest shelf by far, and almost all of it is warm-up music: 1,350 of these 1,429 tracks are filed under the opening hours. Deep house, in this collection, is not a peak-time weapon. It is the sound of the room being built around you. It gets reached for when the night is young and everything still needs to be earned — when the DJ's job is not to excite people but to make them feel, slowly, that they belong here. It is the sound of a door held open.

What does it feel like to be in a room where this is playing? It feels like being let in on something. The vibe vocabulary is almost entirely about interior states: warm, smooth, soulful, atmospheric, introspective. This is late-night music in the true sense — not music that imitates the night, but music that understands the specific melancholy and tenderness of being awake when the rest of the world is asleep. The energy sits at a steady 2, barely rising, never spiking; 1,239 of the 1,429 tracks live exactly there. Nothing here shouts. The collection's deep house asks the listener to lean in, not jump up — to listen the way you listen to someone telling you a story they have never told anyone.

The names on this shelf tell you what kind of deep house it is. Retza leads with 26 tracks — a selector's producer, the kind of name you know because you were in front of a system at the right hour, not because you heard it on the radio. Around him: Just Kiddin, CHRIS STASSY, Dave Pad, Deeplomatik — working producers, track-by-track accumulations, the evidence of years spent digging rather than months spent streaming. Then the elders: St Germain with 10 tracks, Vincenzo with 10, Adriatique with 8 — the lineage made visible, the proof that this shelf has roots. Larry Heard's presence elsewhere in the archive casts a long shadow here too; this is house music that remembers where it came from and behaves accordingly, with soul rather than swagger.

The counts across the shelf taper gently — no single artist running away with it — the shape of years of steady digging rather than one brief obsession. This is a shelf kept alive by curiosity, not completeness.

There is a particular discipline to collecting deep house at this scale. It is not a genre that rewards hoarding — its pleasures are subtle, its differences fine-grained — so 1,429 tracks means the collector has spent an enormous amount of time inside very small distinctions: the exact grain of a Rhodes chord, the precise humidity of a pad, the difference between a vocal that aches and one that merely sighs. The vibe words' quieter end — midnight, morning, sunrise, space, club — sketch the hours this music was collected for: not the night as a party but the night as a place, somewhere you go and stay a while. It is the collector's most personal shelf, and the one that explains all the others. Everything this library does at higher energies, it learned how to do here first: how to hold a room's attention without grabbing it, how to make people feel something without telling them what to feel.

Retza 26 · Just Kiddin 13 · CHRIS STASSY 11 · Dave Pad 11 · Deeplomatik 11 · energy ~2.0 · BPM median 123 (n=716) · Warm-Up

Tech House 910 tracks

If deep house is the room being built, tech house is the room at full occupancy — the peak-time engine of the entire archive. Eight hundred and ninety-eight of these 910 tracks are filed for peak-time; that is as close to unanimous as a shelf gets. This music gets reached for when patience ends and the night needs to move. It is the sound of a DJ who has done the warm-up's work — read the room, earned the trust — and is now cashing it in, track by track, with the confidence of someone holding 910 ways to make a floor erupt. This is the shelf the collector reaches for with total confidence — the crate that never lets a peak hour down.

The feeling is all forward motion. The vibe words are kinetic and unadorned: punchy, rolling, repetitive, minimal, club-driving, momentum. There is no introspection here, no late-night soul-searching — tech house at this scale is a machine for converting sound into sweat. It asks one thing of the listener and it asks it relentlessly: move. The energy centers at 3, with 122 tracks pushing into 4, which tells you this is peak-time with a governor on it — driving but not deranged, the kind of peak that sustains for hours rather than burning out in twenty minutes. The tempo sits at a median of 125, the classic house cruising altitude, fast enough to lift and steady enough to hold. This is music built for the long middle of the night, when the room is full and the DJ's only job is to keep it that way.

The shelf's leaders are craftsmen of exactly that job. Mark Henning (23 tracks) and Dennis Cruz (21) are precision peak-time machinery — producers whose records are tools first and statements second, built for DJs who need a guaranteed reaction at 1:30 a.m. Casey Spillman (11), John Tejada (9), Joshwa (9), Sidney Charles (9), Burnski (8): the roll call reads like a touring DJ's USB stick, names that mean something very specific to anyone who has ever stood in a booth watching a floor and thinking now. Nobody collects 910 tech house tracks by accident; this shelf is an arsenal, and the collector has clearly spent years learning which weapons fire cleanly and which ones jam. The counts taper gently — 23, 21, 11, 9 — the shape of a shelf built by need, each producer kept because their records kept working.

What is interesting is the relationship between this shelf and the deep house ocean next to it. They are the collection's inhale and exhale — 1,429 tracks of warmth and 910 of drive, the two largest genres pulling in opposite emotional directions. The collector's night, read across the two shelves, is a complete argument: begin with soul, arrive at force, never let one exist without the other. The vibe words' quieter tail — disco, moon, sleep, lights, dawn, bounce — even hints at tech house's secret tenderness, the way the best peak-time records carry a flicker of the night's earlier softness inside their drums. But make no mistake about what this shelf is for. It is for the hour when the room is one body, and the body wants to move. It is the sound of the night at its most communal: hundreds of strangers, one rhythm, nobody thinking about anything else.

Mark Henning 23 · Dennis Cruz 21 · Casey Spillman 11 · John Tejada 9 · Joshwa 9 · energy ~3.0 · BPM median 125 (n=602) · Peak-Time

Organic House 828 tracks

The third pillar of the archive's house trinity, and the one that belongs to the daylight. Eight hundred and nineteen of these 828 tracks are warm-up music — but a different warm-up than deep house's late-night interiors. Organic house is for the hours when the light is doing the work: the open-air afternoon, the terrace at golden hour, the morning after that nobody wants to end. It gets reached for when the night has exhaled and the day is coming in, and it is the collection's gentlest argument that the dance floor does not need darkness to be sacred.

To be in a room — or better, a field, a rooftop, a beach — where this is playing is to feel the tempo of your own breathing slow down to match it. The vibe words read like a weather report for a perfect day: organic, percussive, melodic, laid-back, sunlit, warm. This is music made of wood and skin and air rather than steel and strobe: hand drums and shakers, flutes and plucked strings, melodies that unspool instead of stabbing. The energy sits at 2, with a meaningful tail at 1 (134 tracks) and 3 (147) — the widest emotional range of the three house pillars, stretching from near-stillness to genuine lift. It asks the listener for almost nothing and offers almost everything: sway if you want, stand still if you want, close your eyes if you want. Nobody is performing here. Everyone is just present. The median tempo of 122 is the unhurried end of the dance floor — movement as meditation rather than exertion.

The shelf's top names — Arina Mur (10), Makebo (8), Mattias Herrera (8), mredrollo (8), Taleman (8), Wassu (8), Artic White (7), Limara (7) — are not stars but specialists, producers working a seam of sound that barely existed a decade ago and now supports an entire global circuit of sunrise sets and desert festivals. Their even distribution across the shelf (no single dominant artist) says something about how this music was collected: not by following names, but by following a feeling, track by track, wherever it led. The collector heard something — a particular warmth, a particular patience — and kept reaching for it until 828 records had accumulated, each one a small vote for the same idea. This is collecting as attunement: the ear tuned to a frequency, the hand reaching for it again and again.

That idea is the collection's quiet thesis. Deep house gives the archive its soul, tech house its drive, and organic house gives it its light. The three shelves together describe a complete philosophy of the dance floor across the full cycle of a day: the night's interior warmth, the night's kinetic peak, and the day's open-air ease. The vibe words' softer edge — space, clouds, sky, breath, stars, lights — reads like the track titles of the hours after sunrise, when the music is no longer driving anyone anywhere and is simply keeping them company while the world comes back. Of all the archive's large genres, this is the one that feels most like a gift the collector gives themselves: 828 reminders that the best part of the night is sometimes the part where it ends. It is the only one of the three pillars that could be played at noon — and the collector clearly does.

Arina Mur 10 · Makebo 8 · Mattias Herrera 8 · mredrollo 8 · Taleman 8 · energy ~2.0 · BPM median 122 (n=539) · Warm-Up

Eclectic / Other 596 tracks

Every honest library has a shelf for the tracks that refused a shelf, and this is it: 596 records that the genre system could not place, filed together not because they sound alike but because they belong to no one but themselves. Be honest about what this means — there is no fake genre identity here, no invented scene. These are the beautiful miscellany, the strays and orphans and one-offs, and they get reached for the way you reach for the book with no spine label: when you want to be surprised. The moment lean says warm-up (544 of 596), which tells you exactly how the collector uses this shelf — as the wild card in the opening hour, the record nobody expects that somehow makes the whole set make sense.

What does the miscellany feel like? The honest answer is: it depends on the track, and that is the point. But the aggregate has a character anyway. The energy is overwhelmingly 2 — 585 of 596 tracks — which means the strays are not chaos; they are curiosities with manners. The vibe words the system reached for are revealing in their vagueness: eclectic, varied, unpredictable, mixed, leftfield. These are not descriptions of a sound; they are admissions of defeat, and there is something touching about that. The quieter words sketch a mood underneath the variety — sunset, summer, midnight, beach, sunrise, space, horizon — which suggests the miscellany leans warm and open, records collected for their feeling rather than their function. This is the shelf of the collector's private enthusiasms, the things loved too specifically to file.

Look at the names and you see a crate-digger's fingerprint, not a scene's. Beamic (5), home alone. (5), Nuru MacNamara (5), Champagne Romance (4), Mtbrd (4), Vibes & Tones (4), Dreyma (3) — and then, gloriously, George Benson (3), a jazz-funk immortal surfacing among the unknowns like a message from another library entirely. No artist dominates; the deepest commitment is five tracks. This is what a shelf looks like when it is built one record at a time, each chosen because it did something no other record did. The collector's taste is legible everywhere else in the archive by genre; here it is legible only by instinct. You can learn more about a listener from their miscellany than from their main shelves — the main shelves tell you what they believe, the miscellany tells you what they love, and the two are not always the same thing.

There is a discipline in keeping a miscellany this large, too. The easy move with 596 unclassifiable tracks is to force them onto shelves where they do not belong, to tidy the library into a lie. The collector did not do that. They let the strays stay stray, gave them an honest name — eclectic, other — and kept reaching for them in the warm-up hour, where a leftfield record can change the temperature of a whole night. In a 56-genre archive, the 57th genre is the collector themselves: the part of the taste that no taxonomy can hold. This shelf is not a failure of organization. It is the shelf that proves the collector listens with their whole self, not just their DJ brain. There is no tempo data for this shelf — the Spotify-sourced strays carry no BPMs — which feels appropriate: this music was never about the metronome.

House 579 tracks

The plain-named shelf, and the archive's conscience. When a genre is just called "house" — no prefix, no qualifier — it means the root, the source, the thing everything else is a variation on. Four hundred and ninety of these 579 tracks are peak-time records, which tells you this shelf is not a museum; it is a working arsenal of the classics and their descendants, reached for when the night needs not novelty but certainty. This is the music a DJ plays when the floor is full and the only wrong move is a clever one. It gets reached for the way you reach for a handshake: direct, warm, understood by everyone in the room.

The feeling is the feeling of the thing itself, undiluted. The vibe words are the genre's own self-portrait, and they have not needed updating in decades: classic, groovy, jacking, uplifting, dancefloor, timeless. This is music that does exactly what it says — it grooves, it jacks, it uplifts — with the confidence of a form that has been proving itself on dance floors since before most of the archive's other genres existed. The energy centers at 3 (500 of 579 tracks), the honest working energy of a proper house set: driving enough to move a room, human enough to keep it. To be in a room where this is playing is to feel a very old and very simple contract being honored — the DJ gives you rhythm, you give the DJ your body, everybody keeps their end of the bargain. There is a reason the word timeless appears in the vocabulary. Some of these records will still be doing this job in another thirty years.

The shelf's twin pillars say everything about its character: Larry Heard and Mr. Fingers, 12 tracks each — two names for the same immortal, the man who essentially invented deep house, filed here at the root where he belongs. Around them, the lineage continues in both directions: Chaos In The CBD (6) carrying the torch for the new school of warm, musical house; CINTHIE (5), ANOTR (4), ESSEL (4), Franky Rizardo (4), Ian Pooley (4) representing the contemporary underground that still measures itself against the classics. The quieter vibe words — sky, midnight, warehouse, peace, club, disco — sketch the full span of the house tradition, from the Chicago warehouse to the open sky. This shelf is the archive's memory: everything the collector knows about the dance floor, they learned from records like these.

It matters that this shelf exists at this size, distinct from deep house and tech house and all the prefixed variations. It means the collector maintains a relationship with the root — not just the branches they personally prefer, but the trunk everything grew from. The plain house shelf is where the taste shows its respect. In a library of 56 genres and 6,419 tracks, the 534 filed under the simplest possible name are a statement of values: that before the night gets sophisticated, before it gets minimal or melodic or organic, it has to groove — and groove is not a style, it is a discipline. This is the music the collector would play if the power came back on and there was only one crate left.

Minimal / Deep Tech 384 tracks

The afterhours begins here. Three hundred and seventy-six of these 384 tracks are filed for the afterhours — the most single-minded moment assignment of any shelf in the archive — which means this music has essentially one job and does it with total commitment. It gets reached for when the night has thinned to its essence: the tourists have gone home, the lights have come up halfway, and the only people left are the ones who came for the music itself. Minimal / deep tech is what a DJ plays when they no longer have to impress anyone and can finally play. This is the collector's most single-minded shelf — and single-mindedness, at 4 a.m., is a virtue.

The feeling is hypnosis, administered carefully. The vibe words are the archive's most stripped-down: stripped, hypnotic, rolling, late-night, minimal, dubby. This is music that works by subtraction — fewer elements, more space, each sound given room to breathe and repeat until it becomes part of your nervous system. The energy sits at 3, not from intensity but from lock-in: 311 tracks at that level, with only a whisper at 4. To be in a room where this is playing is to feel time change shape; tracks stop being songs and become environments, loops stop being repetitions and become mantras. It asks the listener for the one thing modern life never gives: sustained, unhurried attention. In return it gives the deepest physical pleasure the archive offers — the feeling of your body moving without your mind having to decide anything. It is music that trusts the dancer completely.

Ben Rau dominates this shelf with 27 tracks — the second-deepest artist commitment in the entire collection, and the clearest evidence that this is not a casual interest but a devotion. Around him: Nick Beringer (12), LondonGround (8), Casey Spillman (7), Traumer (7), Diego Krause (6), James Dexter (6), Sublee (6) — the international guild of the reduced groove, producers whose names are passwords among afterhours faithful. The tempo median of 127 keeps the pulse just above house's cruising altitude: urgent without being frantic, the heartbeat of a night that refuses to end. The quieter vibe words — trip, sleep, moon, morning, dawn, club — sketch the exact hours this music owns, the ones where the sky starts changing color and nobody in the room wants to be the first to leave. This shelf is the collector's 4 a.m. self, and they clearly like who they are at 4 a.m.

Progressive House 259 tracks

The long game, filed for the small hours. Two hundred and forty of these 259 tracks belong to the afterhours, which makes progressive house the archive's other great devotion of the late night — but where minimal / deep tech hypnotizes, progressive narrates. It gets reached for when the DJ wants to take the remaining room somewhere: not a track but a trajectory, not a moment but a movement. This is the music of the journey the collection keeps promising, played out at full length while the night dissolves around it.

The feeling is gradual by design. The vibe words read like instructions for patience: gradual, evolving, melodic, journey, emotional, atmospheric. Progressive house does not do drops; it does arrivals — a melody that takes eight minutes to fully reveal itself, a breakdown that feels earned because the track spent its whole life building toward it. The energy sits at 3, with a meaningful push into 4 (30 tracks): this is the afterhours at its most openly emotional, the hour when restraint gives way to release and the room allows itself to feel something. To be in a room where this is playing is to be inside a story someone is telling very slowly, on purpose, because the slowness is the point. It asks the listener to surrender the need to know where it is going. The destination, when it comes, is always worth it.

Trilucid leads with 13 tracks, Stan Kolev follows with 9 — and Kolev's presence in the archive's overall top 15 tells you this shelf punches above its weight in the collector's affections. Quivver (7), djimboh (6), Guy J (5): the names are the genre's modern priesthood, producers who treat the long-form track as a sacred format in an age of the skip button. The quieter vibe words — memories, paradise, stars, midnight, sunrise, clouds — are the most romantic in the archive, and they describe exactly what this music is for: the hours when the night stops being a party and becomes a memory being made in real time. Of all the shelves, this is the one most about time itself — how it stretches, how it heals, how a single well-built hour can feel like a whole life.

Lo-Fi / Chill 252 tracks

The morning after, in full. Two hundred and fifty of these 252 tracks are filed for chill-out — the purest moment assignment in the archive, a shelf with essentially no other job. This music gets reached for when the night is over and the only thing left to do is be gentle with yourself: the drive home, the couch at dawn, the headphones on a slow afternoon. It is the collection's softest landing, and the fact that the collector filed 252 tracks here — a shelf the size of a whole genre — says they take the comedown as seriously as the peak.

The feeling is warmth without demand. The vibe words are a blanket: mellow, dusty, nostalgic, relaxing, warm, hazy. Lo-fi is music that sounds like it has already been lived in — vinyl crackle, tape hiss, chords that blur at the edges like a memory you are not sure is yours. The energy is 1 across the entire shelf, all 252 tracks, the lowest possible setting: this is the only large genre in the archive that never once raises its voice. It asks nothing of the listener. Not attention, not movement, not even wakefulness. It just keeps you company while you come back to yourself. The quieter words — golden, sunshine, sunset, summer, horizon, smooth — sketch the light it was made for: the soft kind, the kind that comes through curtains.

The shelf's architects are the beat-tape underground: Handbook (9), Deeb (8), ELWD (7), Remulak (7), Swørn (6), GlobulDub (5), Guggenz (5) — producers working in small rooms with samplers and patience, making music for nobody's dance floor and everybody's headphones. Note what is absent from the data: no tempo information at all, the Spotify-sourced shelf with nothing to prove about BPM. That absence is fitting. This music does not care how fast it is; it cares how it feels, and it feels like exhaling. In an archive built around the arc of a night, the lo-fi shelf is the epilogue the whole story was heading toward — proof that the collector knows the night only means something because the morning exists, and the morning deserves its own music.

Handbook 9 · Deeb 8 · ELWD 7 · Remulak 7 · Swørn 6 · energy ~1.0 · no tempo data · Chill-Out

Dance / Pop 201 tracks

The celebration shelf. One hundred and ninety-six of these 201 tracks are peak-time records, and the energy tells you what kind of peak: 4, the highest of any large genre in the archive, with 12 tracks pushing all the way to 5. This music gets reached for when the night needs not subtlety but joy — hands in the air, voices singing along, the whole room grinning at itself. It is the collector's least guarded shelf, and every archive needs one: the place where taste steps aside and fun takes over.

The feeling is brightness, polished to a shine: catchy, upbeat, celebratory, polished, singalong, bright. This is music engineered for the moment a roomful of strangers becomes a choir — hooks you know after one listen, production so clean it gleams. It asks the listener for exactly one thing: let go. No patience required, no arc to follow, no subtlety to decode. The quieter words — together, pump, forever, summer, festival, rush — describe the fantasy at the center of every great pop-dance record: that this feeling could last forever, that the summer could never end, that everyone here will remember this. Sometimes the fantasy is true for exactly as long as the track lasts, and that is enough.

Bonus Points (7) and Jones Meadow (6) lead the crossover specialists — D.O.D, Dillon Francis, ODESZA, Mr. Carmack — fluent in both the underground and the main stage. The collector's relationship with this shelf is refreshingly unpretentious: 201 tracks is not a guilty pleasure, it is a pleasure, filed without apology next to the minimal techno. That is the mark of a mature taste: the singalong and the hypnotic loop are not opposites but siblings — two technologies for the same job, making a roomful of people feel, together, that everything is going to be fine.

Bonus Points 7 · Jones Meadow 6 · D.O.D 4 · Dillon Francis, BabyJake 4 · ODESZA 4 · energy ~4.0 · BPM median 124 (n=92) · Peak-Time

Melodic House & Techno 196 tracks

The afterhours at its most cinematic. One hundred and eighty-seven of these 196 tracks are filed for the late night, which places this shelf beside minimal and progressive in the archive's 2 a.m. trinity — but where minimal hypnotizes the body and progressive narrates the night, melodic house and techno goes for the heart. It gets reached for when the room is down to its essence and the remaining dancers deserve something beautiful: not just groove, but grandeur.

The feeling is scale — emotional scale. The vibe words are the archive's most filmic: cinematic, atmospheric, emotional, moody, sophisticated, deep. These are tracks built like scenes: wide synth vistas, melodies that ache, breakdowns like a camera pulling back. The energy sits at 3, steady and held, with 22 tracks reaching toward 4 for the moments when beauty needs force behind it. To be in a room where this is playing is to feel the night acquire meaning — as if the dancing were not just dancing but something closer to ceremony. It asks the listener to feel deeply in public. The quieter words — lights, horizon, ecstasy, neon, rain — sketch the cinema of it: neon on wet pavement, the horizon at 5 a.m.

RÜFÜS DU SOL (6) leads — proof this sound can fill arenas without losing its soul. Behind them the underground's melodic elite: Enamour (4), Marsh (3), Rodriguez Jr. (3), Tale Of Us (3), ARTBAT (2) — names that mean, to the faithful, a very specific shade of blue. In the archive's arc, this shelf is the afterhours' emotional climax: the warm-up was generous, the peak physical, the minimal hours devotional — and here the night gets its catharsis.

RÜFÜS DU SOL 6 · Enamour 4 · Marsh 3 · Rodriguez Jr. 3 · Tale Of Us 3 · energy ~3.0 · BPM median 124 (n=146) · Afterhours

Jazz-Hop / Lo-Fi Hip-Hop 140 tracks

This is the music for after the day lets go — lamp light, a cold cup of tea, the city exhaled somewhere below the window. Nearly every track here (139 of 140) is tagged for chill-out, and the tag is honest: this shelf exists for the hours when ambition is over and attention can soften.

The sound is dusty by design: jazzy chord turns, vinyl-crackle loops, drums that shuffle instead of march — mellow, nostalgic, smooth, and laid-back in exactly that order. Sweatson Klank leads the shelf with eleven tracks of unhurried sample work; Birocratic and El Jazzy Chavo bring the same Sunday-morning ease, while Moods, CrazyJaZz, Flitz&Suppe, Freddie Joachim, and parkbreezy each contribute their own shade of warm haze. Nothing here demands anything of you — it drifts, poolside-soft, with the occasional patter of rain in the corners, and rewards the listener who has nowhere to be. All of it sits at the library's lowest energy tier — the sound of thought slowing down on purpose.

Sweatson Klank ×11 · Birocratic ×7 · energy ~1 (the lowest shelf) · dominant moment: Chill-Out

Techno (Peak Time / Driving) 139 tracks

This is the moment the night stops being social and starts being physical — the room darkens, the lights drop to a strobe pulse, and the floor fills with people who came to move, not to talk. With 135 of 139 tracks tagged peak-time, this shelf has one job: the biggest hour of the night.

Pounding, driving, relentless — the vocabulary here doesn't mince words, and neither does the music. Kick drums land like hammers at a median 126 BPM, hi-hats slice through the density, and every bar pushes forward with high-energy, peak-hour intent. Adam Beyer, Child, Glimpse, and Harvey McKay are the most frequent guides, joined by Andre Michelle, Beckers;D-Nox, Dana Murad, and Dana Ruh — names that read like a roll call of warehouses and raves. There is nothing decorative here: no melody to hide behind, just momentum, pressure, and the shared certainty of a crowd moving as one. This is rave music in the classic sense — less listened to than endured together.

Adam Beyer ×4 · Child ×3 · energy ~4 (high) · BPM median 126 · dominant moment: Peak-Time

Electronica 132 tracks

This is the afterhours shelf — the 2 AM to sunrise stretch when the club has thinned and the conversation moves inward. Tagged afterhours 128 times out of 132, this music belongs to the headphones, the long walk home, and the quiet rooms where sound gets examined rather than consumed.

Experimental, textural, intricate — electronica here is music for close listening, detailed enough to reward a good pair of speakers and strange enough to keep them working. Tycho's sunlit circuitry and Session Victim's dusty machine-funk anchor the shelf, with Apollo 440, Captain Planet and Chico Mann, and Youandewan each adding their own leftfield dialect. At a median 114 BPM it moves like thought: unhurried, layered, occasionally surfacing a melody before diving back into the grain. This is the sound of the night folding back on itself, beautiful and a little unresolved.

Latin / Bachata 105 tracks

All 105 tracks lean the same way: warm-up — the early hours when the room is still filling and the dance floor hasn't committed yet. But bachata warm-up is a particular kind of slow burn: romantic, sensual, swaying, tender. This is the music of the first dance of the night, bodies learning each other in three steps.

Intimate guitar lines, soft percussion, and voices that stay close to the microphone — the palette is smooth and unhurried, built for proximity. Raulin Rodriguez anchors the shelf with twenty tracks, followed by Yoskar Sarante and Zacarias Ferreira, with Anthony Santos, Aventura, El Chaval de la Bachata, Frank Reyes, and Joe Veras rounding out a classic bachata canon. The vocabulary — dembow, percussive, seductive, bass-heavy, club — describes music engineered for bodies in motion: catchy hooks, hips-first rhythms, and bass that you feel in your ribs. Country 86 tracks

Storytelling first, everything else second: heartfelt, twangy, warm, nostalgic, honest. Colter Wall and Tyler Childers lead with thirteen tracks each, Zach Bryan follows with ten, and the lineage runs through Dwight Yoakam, John Prine, Marty Robbins, and Dolly Parton — voices that carry their miles openly. Low energy throughout, but never empty: this is music that sits next to you and tells you what happened, plainly, like an old friend.

How a language model organizes music

Somewhere along the way, the biggest music library in the world quietly stopped organizing itself by genre. Open Spotify on a Tuesday afternoon and it does not ask whether you want techno or jazz. It offers you a daylist — "your day in a playlist," in Spotify's own phrase — a sequence that updates several times between sunup and sundown, because the person you are at 7 a.m. is not the person you are at 11 p.m. The tracks are chosen from your listening patterns; the headline is the breakthrough. Yearning cottagecore thursday afternoon. 90s rave rainforest late night. These oddly perfect titles are generated from your habits crossed with Spotify's enormous map of microgenres, and they do something a genre tree never could: they describe music the way a friend would — in plain feeling-words, aimed at a moment.

The same instinct drives the AI DJ, launched in early 2023. Under the hood it layers large language models and generative voice — spoken in an AI-generated version of Spotify executive Xavier "X" Jernigan's voice — over the company's recommendation machinery, and it behaves less like a playlist than a late-night radio host: sequencing tracks, then narrating the transitions in words, drawing on an in-house knowledge base of music experts. It does not just know what you like. It knows how to talk about what you like — the way a DJ reads a room and says, in effect, here is where the night goes next.

The machinery beneath both is worth a glance. As reported from Spotify's 2026 Investor Day, the company's "Large Taste Model" is trained on some 3.4 trillion daily taste signals, and its job is to predict what you will want to hear next the way a chatbot predicts the next word. The core idea is an embedding: every track becomes a point in a vast space, placed near other tracks not only because they sound alike, but because people reach for them in similar contexts. Spotify Research publishes openly in this territory — including contrastive audio-language work that learns cross-modal embeddings linking the audio and text domains — and the wider research field has followed: models like MusCALL, presented at ISMIR 2022, train dual audio-and-language encoders so you can type a sentence and get back sound, or feed in sound and get back words, even classifying genres zero-shot by simply offering the labels as text. The shared insight is that language is the bridge. Once a system can describe "late-night, warm-up energy" the way a DJ would, rigid genre trees stop being the organizing principle. The moment is.

Which brings us, honestly, to this archive. Pico Nebula does none of that. It has no embeddings, no audio analysis, no language models — it has never heard a single one of these 6,419 tracks. It has only ever read their labels. What it does is a metadata-estimated echo of the same philosophy: every track is tagged with a moment (warm-up, peak-time, afterhours, chill-out, closing), an energy level from 1 to 5, and a handful of vibe words — estimates from BPM, genre and title, not audio analysis. The industry builds embeddings from sound to arrive at "late-night"; this archive walks backward from metadata to approximate the same idea. The contrast is the point. One approach measures the music; the other reads its sleeve notes. But both have landed on the same conviction: a library is best organized not by the shelf it sits on, but by the moment you are in. That is why the Taste tab leads with moments and vibe words — the feeling, not the filing cabinet.
